meta.note: ترجمةٌ مولَّدةٌ بمراجعة عددٍ وترتيب — الاقتباساتُ ترجمةُ معنًى لا نصًّا محكَّمًا

ata-jaa.title: The Semantic Nuances of ata and ja'a
ata-jaa.kashf: The verb "جاء" (ja'a) appears exclusively in the past tense throughout the Quran (278/278 instances); wherever the context necessitated the present tense or imperative of this meaning, "أتى" (ata) was employed.
readings: Al-Ityān (coming) is an arrival with ease... and al-Majī' (coming) is like al-Ityān, but al-Majī' is more general; for al-Ityān may be used with consideration of intention even if the attainment does not occur, while al-Majī' is used with consideration of actual attainment.
'Atā' is used for what is easier, and 'Jā'a' for what involves difficulty or hardship—and 'Jā'a' has not appeared in the Qur'an in the imperfect tense, nor as a command, nor as an active participle.

khawf-khashya.title: A Comparative Semantic Study of khawf and khashya
khawf-khashya.kashf: "الخشية" (reverential awe) is predominantly directed towards God (the divine name appearing 41 times in its 40 verses), whereas "الخوف" (general fear) is associated with punishment, the Day (of Judgment), and various circumstances.
readings: Al-Khashyah (reverent fear) pertains to the one who brings about the disliked thing, and fear of the disliked thing itself is not called khashyah; for this reason, He said: 'And they fear their Lord and dread the evil of the reckoning.'

Al-Khashyah is a fear mixed with veneration, and mostly this arises from knowledge of that which is feared; for this reason, scholars are singled out for it: 'Only those who have knowledge among His servants fear Allah.'

istataa.title: The Linguistic Distinction Between ista'u and istata'u
istataa.kashf: The verb "استطاع" (to be able) appears in its shortened form (without the 'ta') only twice, both in Surah Al-Kahf, and both adjacent to its full form—the lighter construction signifying an easier action.
readings: 'Wastā'ū' is a lighter form of 'Istaṭā'ū', and combining them is an artistic variation in the eloquence of speech... And among the characteristics of deviating from the apparent meaning here is preferring a verb with an increase in structure in a context where there is an increase in meaning, because the ability to bore through the dam is stronger than the ability to climb it.

Hamza recited with a shaddah on the ṭā', and the others with a light ṭā'... Al-Zajjāj said: 'Whoever recites thus is mistaken and errs in grammar.' And al-A'shā recited from Abu Bakr: 'Iṣṭā'ū' by substituting the sīn with a ṣād.

qasit-muqsit.title: The Semantic Contrast of al-qasitun and al-muqsitun
qasit-muqsit.kashf: The triliteral verb "قسَط" (qasata) denotes injustice in its two Meccan occurrences, while the quadriliteral "أقسط" (aqsat) signifies justice in all eight of its Medinan occurrences, each within legal injunctions.
readings: Al-Qisṭ (with kasrah) is to take another's share, and that is injustice; and al-Iqsāṭ is to give another's share, and that is fairness; for this reason, it is said: 'The man qasaṭa (was unjust) when he acted unjustly, and aqsaṭa (was fair) when he acted justly.'
Qasaṭa: he was unjust. He is a qāsiṭ (unjust one), not a muqsiṭ (just one). And Allah commanded al-qisṭ (justice) and forbade al-qasṭ (injustice).

basair.title: Basair: Clear Proofs and Profound Insights in the Quran
basair.kashf: The term "بصائر" (enlightening insights) is exclusively applied in the Quran to revealed scripture—the Quran or the Book of Moses—always coupled with guidance and mercy; all seven of its occurrences are Meccan.
readings: The perceptive power of the heart is called baṣīrah (insight) and baṣar (sight)... And the plural of baṣīrah is baṣā'ir, and the physical eye is hardly ever called baṣīrah.
Al-Baṣīrah is the intellect by which meanings and realities become manifest... And attributing 'coming' to baṣā'ir (insights) is a metaphor for their occurrence in their minds.

aam-sana.title: A Comparative Semantic Study of am and sanah
aam-sana.kashf: "السنة" (year) is predominantly mentioned in contexts of hardship and trial, whereas "العام" (year) is mostly associated with ease and prosperity—and they converge in the verse of Noah, highlighting this very contrast.
readings: Often, 'sanah' (year) is used for a year in which there is hardship or drought, and 'ām' (year) for what contains prosperity and fertility... And in 'a thousand years save fifty years' there is a subtle point.
He expressed with the word 'sanah' (year) as a dispraise for the days of disbelief, and he said 'ām' (year) as an indication that his time after their drowning was pleasant, expansive, and good.

rih-riyah.title: The Semantic Nuances of rih and riyah in the Quran
rih-riyah.kashf: All plural occurrences of "الرياح" (winds) (10/10) appear in contexts of mercy and revival; conversely, the singular form is mostly used for severity, with exceptions confined to specific types.
readings: In most places where Allah mentioned the sending of wind (al-rīḥ) in the singular, it refers to punishment, and in every place where it is mentioned in the plural (al-riyāḥ), it refers to mercy.

Al-Rīḥ (wind/scent/power) in the Qur'an has three meanings: the wind itself ('And the changing of the winds'), the scent ('Indeed, I perceive the scent of Joseph'), and the power ('And your strength departs').

matar-ghayth.title: A Comparative Semantic Analysis of matar and ghayth
matar-ghayth.kashf: The verb "أمطر" (to rain down) is exclusively used for divine punishment, while "الغيث" (beneficial rain) is solely used for good; when "مطر" (ordinary rain) is mentioned, it appears in contexts of hardship, not retribution.
readings: It is said that 'maṭar' (rain) is used for good, and 'amṭara' (to rain down) for punishment: 'And We rained upon them a rain, and evil was the rain of those who were warned'... And al-ghawth is used for assistance, and al-ghayth for rain.
Al-Maṭar (rain) in the Qur'an has two meanings: the known rain ('There was harm to you from rain'), and stones ('And We rained upon them a rain' in the story of the people of Lot).

bukhl-shuhh.title: The Nuances of bukhl and shuhh: A Comparative Study
bukhl-shuhh.kashf: "البخل" (stinginess) is attributed to the act of withholding what God has bestowed, whereas "الشح" (avarice) is ascribed to the soul and disposition—appearing as "شح نفسه" (the avarice of his soul) in both its instances, all of which are Medinan.
readings: Al-Shuḥḥ is eagerness to withhold good... And al-Bukhl is withholding what is due.
Al-Shuḥḥ is stinginess combined with eagerness, and that is in what was customary.

nima-naim.title: A Comparative Semantic Study of ni'mah and na'im
nima-naim.kashf: "النعيم" (ultimate bliss) refers exclusively to the bliss of the Hereafter (17/17); "النِّعمة" (favor/blessing, with kasra) denotes a state applicable to both worlds; and "النَّعمة" (worldly luxury, with fatḥa) signifies blameworthy worldly indulgence in its two occurrences.
readings: Al-Ni'mah (with kasrah) is the good state, and its form is that of a state noun; and al-Na'mah (with fatḥah) is enjoyment, and its form is that of a noun of single instance from the verb.
As for al-Na'mah—with a fatḥah on the nūn—it is enjoyment, and the one who enjoys is the one who lives in luxury.

rafa-rahma.title: The Nuances of ra'fah and rahmah: A Comparative Study
rafa-rahma.kashf: Wherever "الرأفة" (compassion) and "الرحمة" (mercy) are conjoined, "الرأفة" is invariably presented first; the phrase "رحيم رءوف" (Merciful, Compassionate) never occurs; and "الرحمة" possesses an unparalleled breadth (114 instances).
readings: Al-Ra'fah (compassion) is more intense than al-Raḥmah (mercy); for this reason, Abu 'Ubaydah said regarding 'Ra'ūf, Raḥīm' (Compassionate, Merciful): 'Emphasis is achieved by what is more intense in meaning, so if the more intense in wording precedes, the meaning is then reinforced.'

ahd-mithaq.title: A Comparative Semantic Analysis of ahd and mithaq
ahd-mithaq.kashf: "الميثاق" (solemn covenant) is "taken" (22 times) and described as firm, whereas "العهد" (pledge) is "fulfilled" and "broken"—reflecting a distinction between the solemnization of a moment and a sustained course of commitment.
readings: Al-Mīthāq (solemn covenant) is the confirmation of al-'Ahd (pledge), from your saying 'I made the thing firm' when you tightened its binding securely. And it is said: al-'Ahd is a state between the two parties to the pledge, while al-Mīthāq is from one of them.
Al-'Ahd (pledge) is the preservation of a thing and its observance moment after moment... And al-Mīthāq (solemn covenant) is a contract confirmed by an oath and a pledge.

istafa-ijtaba.title: The Nuances of Divine Selection: istafa, ijtaba, and ikhtara
istafa-ijtaba.kashf: "اصطفى" (to choose) elevates above all beings; "اجتبى" (to elect) encompasses and guides (as in "He elected him and guided him"); and "اختار" (to select) denotes picking from a number—all four instances of "اختار" being Meccan.
readings: Al-Iṣṭifā' (selection) is taking the pure essence of a thing, just as al-Ikhtiyār (choice) is taking its best part, and al-Ijtibā' (gathering/choosing) is taking its collected portion—and al-Ijtibā' is gathering by way of selection.

zann-hasiba-zaama.title: A Comparative Semantic Study of dhann, hasib, and za'am
zann-hasiba-zaama.kashf: The verb "زعم" (to claim) appears exclusively in the Quran in contexts of rejected assertions (15/15); "الظن" (conjecture) spans between praiseworthy certainty and blameworthy adherence to speculation; and "الحسبان" (reckoning) denotes an expectation that is condemned.
readings: Al-Za'm is the narration of a statement that is likely to be false, and for this reason, it appeared in the Qur'an in every place where those who utter it are condemned.
Al-Shakk (doubt) is the equality of the two possibilities, and al-Ẓann (conjecture) is the preponderance of one of the two possibilities.

saqa-asqa.title: The Semantic Distinction Between saqa and asqa
saqa-asqa.kashf: The triliteral verb form is used for offering a present drink, while the quadriliteral form is for establishing a permanent source—a distinction consistently observed, letter by letter, across all twenty relevant instances, as noted by Al-Raghib.
readings: Al-Saqy is to give him what he drinks; and al-Isqā' is to make that available to him so that he may take it as he wishes—so al-Isqā' is more intense than al-Saqy, you say: 'I provided him with a river (to drink from).'

badan-jasad.title: A Comparative Semantic Study of badan, jasad, and jism
badan-jasad.kashf: "الجسد" (body), in its four occurrences, refers to a lifeless or inactive corporeal form; "البدن" (body) denotes a specific, tangible physical body; and "الجسم" (body) signifies apparent bulk or size—used for praise when accompanied by knowledge, and for blame when devoid of it.
readings: Al-Badan is said with consideration of the size of the body, and al-Jasad with consideration of the color... And al-Jism is that which has length, width, and depth—'Their bodies impress you' is a warning that there is no significant meaning beyond the physical forms.
'Badan' has two meanings: the body ('We will save you with your body,' meaning with your physical body), and al-Budn (pl.) whose singular is badanah, meaning the fat camels.

halafa-aqsama.title: The Semantic Distinction Between halaf and aqsama
halafa-aqsama.kashf: The verb "حلف" (to swear) appears exclusively in the Quran in contexts of false or excusatory oaths (13/13); whereas "أقسم" (to swear) is the comprehensive term for all oaths, encompassing those of God, the truthful, and the liars.
readings: Al-Ḥilf is the covenant between people, and al-Muḥālafah is the mutual covenanting, and it is made for adherence.

khushu-khudu.title: A Comparative Semantic Study of khushu and khudu
khushu-khudu.kashf: "الخشوع" (humility/devotion) is ascribed to hearts, eyes, and voices, conveying praise and awe (17 instances); whereas "الخضوع" (submission/subservience), in its two occurrences, denotes an outward, unpraised compliance: bowing of necks and softening of speech.
readings: Al-Khushū' is humility/supplication, and it is mostly used for what is manifested on the limbs... And it is said: 'If the heart is humble, the limbs become submissive.'
Al-Khushū' is specifically in speech, and the evidence is His saying, the Most High: 'And voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful.'

fitna.title: Al-Fitnah: An Exegetical Study of Trial and Temptation
fitna.kashf: The Meccan verb "فتن" (to test) adheres to its original sense of testing (e.g., gold by fire), while the Medinan noun "فتنة" (trial/discord) expanded in meaning to encompass polytheism, hindering from faith, and fighting—as in "And *fitnah* is worse than killing."
readings: The origin of al-Fitnah is putting gold into fire to reveal its quality from its impurity, and it is used for putting a human into fire.
Al-Fitnah is the most severe and intense test... And it can be in good and evil: 'Indeed, your wealth and your children are a trial.'

sakina.title: Al-Sakinah: An Exegetical Study of Divine Tranquility
sakina.kashf: "السكينة" (tranquility) is not acquired; rather, it is sent down by God upon hearts in moments of fear, and all six of its occurrences are Medinan.
readings: Al-Sakīnah is the departure of agitation during anger and fear, and it mostly appeared in the context of fear... And it is attributed to the heart: 'It is He who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers.'
And Allah, the Most High, mentioned al-Sakīnah in six places.
